sources.name: CWE catalogue entries examined by hand for a pure-Elixir bit-validation library. MITRE publishes language views for C, C++ and Java, among others, and no Elixir-specific view is known to this review, so no view id is cited and no member-list snapshot exists; the considered_not_included list is a reviewer list, not a view walk (VER15a section 9 rule 9 cannot be checked for this lane)

Elixir and BEAM language pitfalls: strict versus loose equality (1.0 == 1, 1.0 !== 1), guards and pattern-match failures (FunctionClauseError, MatchError, a guard that raises simply fails), atoms and the atom table, arbitrary-precision integers, Inspect and String.Chars protocol dispatch on caller structs, Code.eval_*, :erlang.binary_to_term, apply/3, the process dictionary, Application env, :persistent_term and ETS, runtime module redefinition, heap growth without a stack overflow, descending default ranges, Hex lock and publish rules
LG02 sections 7 and 9: error identity and the type-confusion matrix (elixir rows; the section 7 row 12 and section 9 row are stale after PR #19952)

This repo's audits of the elixir lane: LGE-R-elixir (PR #19952, merged 2026-11-24: InvalidBitError, exhaustive tests), LGE-DOS-ALL (queued; names every lane with these blocks), and by-hand probes of this review on Elixir 1.19.5 (OTP 28): mux_n with three inputs, demux with n_outputs 0 and -3, mux4 with a struct whose Inspect implementation prints a marker, and_n over 2,000,000 bits, decoder over 16 bits, counter reset with a garbage state, a runtime redefinition of the transistors module, and one mix test --cover run (166 tests, 95.28% line coverage)

threats.name: Use After Free
threats.rationale: The BEAM garbage-collects every term and exposes no manual free, so a use after free needs native memory: a NIF or port driver loaded into the VM. A pure-Elixir package has no deallocator it controls. By reading, neither the package nor the transistors dependency loads native code (no :erlang.load_nif, Port, Rustler or Zigler in lib/).

threats.name: Integer Overflow to Buffer Boundary
threats.rationale: This registry class is wraparound that leads to a wrong buffer size or offset. Elixir integers are arbitrary precision and never wrap, so no integer arithmetic here can overflow into a buffer boundary; the one place a width appears is a bitstring segment (<<x::8>> truncates silently), and the package has no bitstring literal. Bitwise.bsl(1, length(inputs)) (combinational.ex:337) cannot overflow but a large caller-chosen length makes a huge integer and a huge list, which is the resource row elixir.input-size-heap-growth, not this one. Release text must render the full registry name, never "integer overflow excluded".

threats.name: Code Injection / Eval
threats.rationale: Elixir can compile and run text or data as code (Code.eval_*, Code.compile_*, Code.require_file), build atoms and modules from data (String.to_atom, Module.concat, Module.create), decode terms that carry functions (:erlang.binary_to_term) and call a computed module and function (apply/3, a variable-module call). The v2 subset no_dynamic_eval_reachable (VER15a section 1.3) gives the class an exclusion route under fail-closed semantics: an over-approximating analyzer rule plus a seeded negative-control corpus, both live. By reading, the library calls none of them (a grep of lib/ in both packages finds no Code., apply, binary_to_term, String.to_atom, Module. or variable-module call); apply/3 appears only in the test file (gates_exhaustive_test.exs:90, :96, :106), which is an evidence producer, not part of the claim.

closed_by.detail: Over-approximating call-graph rule (VER15a section 1.3(a)): every call target resolved to a constant, none an evaluation primitive; an unresolved variable-module call (mod.fun(...)), Function.capture/3 or apply with a computed module or function is itself a finding. Primitive list (closed, versioned, minimum per section 1.3(c)): Code.eval_string, Code.eval_quoted, Code.eval_file, Code.compile_string, Code.compile_quoted, Code.compile_file, Code.require_file, Code.load_file, macros that evaluate caller data, :erlang.binary_to_term, String.to_atom and Module.concat on caller data, :erlang.apply, apply/3 and apply/2 with a computed module or function; this lane adds Module.create, :code.load_binary/:code.load_file, :erlang.load_module and List.to_atom/:erlang.binary_to_atom. Transitive dependencies are in the call graph (the transistors package). Build, mix-task and install hooks belong to elixir.build-and-hex-hygiene, not this rule.

Seeded negative control (VER15a section 1.3(b)): a planted instance of every primitive in the list above, each directly and via indirection (an alias, a callback, a captured function, apply with a variable module), and the rule must flag every one. A new primitive needs a new seeded case in the same change.

The package-local part (caps, rejecting n_outputs early) is routed on elixir.input-size-heap-growth (LGE-DOS-ALL, LGE-EX-HARDEN).

threats.name: Uncontrolled Recursion
threats.rationale: The BEAM has no call-stack overflow: a non-tail recursion lives on the process heap and grows until the machine runs out of memory, so uncontrolled recursion shows up as heap growth, not a stack error. threats.name: Prototype Pollution
threats.rationale: Prototype pollution mutates a prototype chain of a JavaScript-style object. Elixir has immutable terms, no objects and no inheritance chain; a loaded module cannot be extended by data. The pair (elixir, 1321) is on the VER15a section 5.5 excluded-by-language whitelist, entered unsigned (signed_off false), and no registry subset covers elixir, so that whitelist entry is the sole authority. The entry excludes the prototype-chain mechanism only: the process dictionary, :persistent_term, ETS and Application env are shared mutable state, which belongs to elixir.shared-runtime-state, and redefining a loaded module belongs to elixir.module-redefinition-and-hot-code-loading.

closed_by.detail: Elixir terms are immutable; there are no objects, classes or prototype chains for a program to extend from input, and a map key written with Map.put/3 produces a new map instead of mutating a shared one. A statement about the language, not a check.

threats.name: Access of Resource Using Incompatible Type (Type Confusion)

threats.name: atoms are never garbage-collected
threats.rationale: Atoms live in a fixed-size global table (about one million by default) and are never freed; creating enough of them from data kills the whole VM. String.to_atom, List.to_atom, :erlang.binary_to_atom and Module.concat on caller data are how that happens. The package converts nothing to an atom: a rejected atom is described by type without being turned into text (gates.ex:90-92) and nothing calls String.to_atom (grep of lib/). The suite passes :a and :"1" (gates_exhaustive_test.exs:61-62), which proves rejection, not that the table does not grow.

closed_by.detail: Library sources call no String.to_atom, List.to_atom, :erlang.binary_to_atom, :erlang.list_to_atom or Module.concat/Module.safe_concat on a value that came from the caller (String.to_existing_atom is also flagged, because it still lets caller data probe the table).

The BEAM garbage-collects every term, terms are immutable, binaries and tuples are bounds-checked (element/2 and binary_part/3 out of range raise ArgumentError), and there is no pointer arithmetic or manual free. A statement about the VM (an accepted baseline), not a check on the package. It holds only while no NIF, port driver or other native code is loaded.

threats.name: process dictionary, Application env, persistent_term and ETS
threats.rationale: The BEAM offers four places to hide mutable state outside the arguments: the process dictionary (Process.put/get), the application environment (Application.put_env), :persistent_term and ETS tables. A library that read configuration from one of them, or cached a result in one, would make a gate's output depend on something other than its arguments, and a caller or another library could change it. The package uses none of them by reading; its state is explicit.

closed_by.detail: Library sources call no Process.put/get/delete, Application.put_env/get_env/fetch_env, :persistent_term, :ets, :atomics or :counters function, and define no module attribute that is read at runtime from the environment.

threats.name: any code in the VM can replace a module

Any code in the same VM can therefore replace Gates or the transistors module, and the gates would then return whatever the replacement returns. This is the in-process analogue of Python monkeypatching and the C lane's caller-side narrowing: the library cannot detect or prevent it.

closed_by.detail: A module loaded in the VM can be redefined at runtime by any code in the same VM; nothing in the language or the package can prevent it. Confirmed by the probe quoted in the rationale.

closed_by.detail: demux enumerates outputs with Enum.map(0..(n_outputs - 1), ...) threats.name: Hex publishing, lock files, coverage gate and test/release divergence
threats.rationale: The Hex supply chain is mix.lock (the pinned versions with checksums) and the Hex registry's package signing. This closure has no Hex dependency, so there is nothing to lock today, and the repository guards would fail a closure that gained one without a lock. Publishing is a separate gap: a path dependency cannot be published, there is no package metadata, the coverage gate is 80 against a 95 target, the test build differs from a release in protocol consolidation, and Windows builds the dependency by a different line. None of these is a weakness class by itself; each decides whether what is tested is what is shipped. Build, mix-task and install hooks are in this row, not in the CWE-94 rule.

closed_by.detail: Repository CI runs python3 code/scripts/elixir_locks.py check (.github/workflows/ci.yml:869) and third_party_dependency_policy.py check --ecosystem elixir (ci.yml:915): a project whose path-dependency closure reaches a Hex dependency must carry a tracked mix.lock with checksums. This closure has none: mix.exs:24-28 lists only the path dependency, and code/packages/elixir/transistors/mix.exs lists deps [] (:24-26); there is no mix.lock. The guards run in the repository contracts job, not as part of a lane report.

mix.exs:26 depends on the transistors package by path (path: "../transistors"), which Hex refuses to publish; mix.exs:4-16 has no description or package metadata; the coverage threshold is 80 (mix.exs:12-14) although the suite measures 95.28%; consolidate_protocols is false in :test only (mix.exs:8), so the test build dispatches protocols differently from a release; BUILD_windows omits the transistors compile line that BUILD has (BUILD:1 versus BUILD_windows:1).

mix.exs gains description, package (licenses, links, files) and a Hex-publishable dependency story: a path: dependency cannot be published to Hex (mix.exs:26), so the transistors package must be published first and referenced by version. Covered by the publish work of LGE-S5 (VER31 amendment) and the per-registry publish jobs; the package-local part is the mix.exs change.

mix.exs test_coverage threshold raised from 80 (mix.exs:12-14) to at least 95 for this package; the built-in mix test --cover is the coverage tool (no ExCoveralls). One local run on Elixir 1.19.5 measured 95.28% total, so the gate would pass today but nothing enforces it.
